basic_identification.name: EU AI Act training data provisions (2026)
basic_identification.originator: European Parliament and Council of the European Union. Key architects: Brando Benifei (MEP, co-rapporteur), Dragos Tudorache (MEP, co-rapporteur). European Commission (Thierry Breton, former Commissioner for Internal Market). European AI Office (established 2024) oversees implementation. Relevant provisions primarily in Articles 53 and 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
basic_identification.year: 2024 (enacted August 1, 2024), 2025 (codes of practice development), 2026 (general-purpose AI model obligations fully applicable from August 2, 2025; full Act enforcement including penalties from August 2, 2026)
basic_identification.geography: European Union (27 member states). Extraterritorial reach: applies to any AI system placed on the EU market or whose output is used in the EU, regardless of where the provider is based. This gives it de facto global impact similar to GDPR. Particularly affects US and Chinese AI companies operating in EU markets.

core_ideas.core_claim: AI providers must be transparent about what data they used to train their models, respect copyright opt-out mechanisms, and clearly label AI-generated content. The EU AI Act's training data provisions establish the principle that AI development is not exempt from existing rights frameworks — copyright holders retain rights over their works even when used as training data, and the public has a right to know when content is AI-generated. This is the most comprehensive regulatory framework for AI training data worldwide.
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Directly relevant to digital art. The training data provisions address the core tension in AI art: generative models are trained on millions of artworks, often without consent or compensation. The provisions make this practice legally regulable for the first time. The copyright opt-out requirement (respecting Article 4 of the DSM Directive's text and data mining exception) and the training data summary requirement create new obligations that specifically affect how AI models that generate images, text, music, and video are developed.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: Disruptive to attention-economy AI. The provisions create friction for AI systems that generate content for engagement (social media content farms, automated marketing, deepfakes). By requiring transparency and copyright compliance, the Act makes attention-economy exploitation of creative works more costly and traceable. However, the provisions do not directly address attention-economy dynamics — they regulate the supply chain (training data) rather than the distribution mechanism (algorithmic amplification).
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: Strongly intention-aligned. The provisions serve declared structural needs of the creative ecosystem: protecting creator rights, ensuring transparency, establishing accountability. This is regulatory infrastructure that supports intention-based cultural production over attention-based content extraction. The Act explicitly recognizes that unregulated AI training creates systemic risk to creative industries and democratic information environments.

market_economics.revenue_model: Regulatory framework — does not generate revenue directly. Affects revenue models of AI companies (compliance costs, licensing requirements). Creates potential revenue streams for rights holders (licensing training data). Funds enforcement through EU AI Office budget and national competent authorities. Penalties for non-compliance: up to 3% of global annual turnover or EUR 15 million for general-purpose AI model providers.
market_economics.market_position: Regulatory infrastructure. Sits above all market participants as a constraint. Defines the rules within which AI art tools, platforms, and markets operate in the EU.
market_economics.price_range: N/A — regulatory framework, not a product or service.
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Increasing enforcement intensity. 2024: Act published. 2025: AI literacy and prohibited practices provisions apply; codes of practice for general-purpose AI models under development. August 2025: general-purpose AI model obligations apply. August 2026: full enforcement including high-risk AI system requirements and penalties. The trajectory is toward increasing regulatory scrutiny and compliance requirements. [uncertain]
market_economics.collector_demographics: N/A — applies to all participants in the AI ecosystem. Most directly affects: AI model developers (OpenAI, Stability AI, Midjourney, Google DeepMind), content platforms, creative professionals whose works are used as training data, and downstream users of AI-generated content.
market_economics.sustainability: Highly sustainable as a regulatory framework. Backed by EU institutional apparatus, enforcement mechanisms, and political will. The Act is law — it does not depend on market sentiment or funding cycles. Sustainability risk: regulatory capture (lobbying dilutes provisions), enforcement gaps (under-resourced national authorities), or technological circumvention (training outside EU jurisdiction). The precedent-setting nature means other jurisdictions may adopt similar provisions, reinforcing durability.

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Not a tool but creates requirements for tools. Affects: AI training pipelines (must implement opt-out compliance), content management systems (must implement AI labeling), generative AI tools (must embed provenance information, compatible with C2PA). Creates demand for new tools: training data auditing systems, copyright compliance checkers, opt-out mechanism implementations (robots.txt, ai.txt, Spawning's Do Not Train registry), AI content detection and labeling systems.
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: This IS regulation of AI. The training data provisions directly govern how generative AI models are built, what data they can use, and how their outputs must be disclosed. Article 53(1)(c) requires providers to put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law, in particular to identify and comply with reservations of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of the DSM Directive. Article 53(1)(d) requires a sufficiently detailed summary of training data content. Article 50 requires AI-generated content to be labeled as such. This is the most significant AI regulation for creative practice globally.
practice_aesthetics.liveness: Regulatory provisions are living documents in practice — interpreted through enforcement actions, court cases, codes of practice, and guidance. The AI Office's codes of practice (under development in 2025-2026) will elaborate the provisions. Not static: the regulatory interpretation evolves as technology evolves.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: Regulatory/legal: training data transparency, copyright opt-out, text and data mining (TDM) exception, sufficiently detailed summary, machine-readable opt-out, AI-generated content labeling, general-purpose AI model (GPAI), systemic risk, fundamental rights. The vocabulary bridges legal, technical, and creative domains but is primarily legal. The aesthetic implications (how does mandatory AI labeling change the perception of AI art?) lack dedicated critical vocabulary.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: Openness vs. enclosure: creates obligations for transparency (openness of process) while protecting enclosure rights (copyright). Commons vs. capture: protects commons (public right to know about AI content) while reinforcing private capture (copyright holders' control over training data). Spectacle vs. infrastructure: purely infrastructure. Individual vs. collective: balances individual rights (creator copyright, user transparency) with collective interests (AI innovation, public safety).

infrastructure_governance.openness: The Act itself is public law, freely accessible. Codes of practice are developed through multi-stakeholder processes with public consultation. Enforcement decisions will be public. However, the training data summaries required from AI providers may be less transparent than advocates hoped — the detail level of 'sufficiently detailed summary' is contested and subject to codes of practice interpretation.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: EU institutional governance: European Commission, European AI Office (enforcement), European Artificial Intelligence Board (coordination of national authorities), national competent authorities (member state level enforcement). Multi-stakeholder input through codes of practice development, public consultations, and expert groups. Democratic accountability through European Parliament oversight.
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: The provisions strengthen creator data sovereignty by requiring respect for copyright opt-out and transparency about training data use. Artists and rights holders can assert control over whether their works are used for AI training. However, enforcement is challenging: how do you verify compliance with opt-out at the scale of internet-wide data scraping? The practical effectiveness of data sovereignty depends on technical implementation of opt-out mechanisms and enforcement capacity.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: The Act references existing standards (C2PA for AI content labeling, DSM Directive for copyright). It does not create its own technical standards but mandates compliance with outcomes, leaving implementation to providers. This approach allows interoperability with existing systems. The AI Office's codes of practice will further specify technical requirements. The Act is designed to work with, not replace, existing IP frameworks.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: Training data summaries create a new archival requirement — documented records of what data was used to train models. This has preservation implications: for the first time, there will be a documented record (however summary) of AI models' cultural inputs. The Act does not directly address preservation of AI-generated art, but AI labeling requirements create metadata that supports future preservation and historicization.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Hybrid opt-out. The default under EU copyright law (DSM Directive Article 4) is that text and data mining for commercial purposes requires an opt-out: rights holders must explicitly reserve their rights, or their works can be used. The AI Act reinforces this opt-out framework and requires AI providers to respect it. This is not opt-in consent (artists must actively refuse rather than actively permit). The opt-out approach has been criticized by artist advocacy groups as insufficient — it places the burden on creators to protect their works rather than requiring AI companies to obtain permission.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: Integration with existing rights frameworks. The Act reinforces traditional copyright principles (artists own their works) and extends them to the AI context. Traditional art world institutions benefit from the protections. The Act does not disrupt the art world — it protects it from AI disruption. Museums, galleries, and collecting societies are stakeholders in the regulatory process.
field_position.what_it_enables: Legal basis for artists to control how their works are used in AI training. Transparency requirements that make AI model composition auditable. Content labeling that helps audiences distinguish AI-generated from human-created work. A framework for licensing and compensation for training data use. Precedent for other jurisdictions to follow. Design constraints for any AI-powered creative tool operating in the EU.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Effective enforcement mechanisms at scale (how to monitor compliance across all AI training globally). Adequate training data summary detail (the 'sufficiently detailed' standard is vague). Retroactive application (existing models trained before the Act are not retroactively regulated). Individual artist compensation mechanism (the Act protects rights but does not create a payment system). Coverage of open-source models (exemptions for open-source complicate enforcement). Adequate resources for national competent authorities to enforce.
field_position.who_is_excluded: Non-EU creators whose works are scraped by non-EU AI companies (extraterritorial enforcement is limited). Artists who do not know about or cannot implement opt-out mechanisms (digital literacy barrier). Small and independent AI developers who may lack resources for compliance. Creators in jurisdictions without equivalent protections (creating a global enforcement gap). Open-source AI communities that benefit from exemptions but whose users may not comply.
field_position.frontier_signal: Established as regulation, frontier in implementation. The Act is law but the practical meaning of the training data provisions is still being determined through codes of practice (2025-2026). The frontier is in implementation: what does 'sufficiently detailed summary' mean in practice? How are opt-out mechanisms technically implemented? How is compliance verified? The answers to these questions in 2026 will determine whether the provisions are transformative or toothless.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: Regulatory compliance requirements (AI companies must discover and implement). Legal press, technology press, art press. EU official publications. Advocacy organizations (European Digital Rights, Communia, artist unions). Conferences and policy forums. Not discovered through social media — discovered through professional and regulatory channels.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: Zero. Regulation does not depend on attention or engagement. The Act applies regardless of whether anyone is paying attention to it. Enforcement is institutional, not attention-driven. This is the opposite of attention-economy logic: compliance is mandatory, not voluntary.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Maximally intention-aligned. Regulation is the purest form of declared structural need: democratic institutions have determined that AI training data transparency and copyright compliance are necessary for the public good. The provisions exist to serve the field's structural needs, not to capture engagement.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: Strong. The Act creates new commons: mandatory training data summaries become public knowledge about AI model composition. AI labeling creates a public information layer about content authenticity. The regulatory framework itself is a commons (public law, freely accessible). However, the Act also reinforces private enclosure (copyright) — the tension between commons and enclosure is managed, not resolved.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Both, indirectly. The Act requires provenance of AI model training (what data was used — a form of creation provenance) and provenance of AI-generated content (labeling — a form of origin marking). It does not track provenance of meaning, but the training data summaries create a new form of cultural provenance: what cultural inputs produced what AI capabilities.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Regulatory temporality: phased implementation (2024-2026), with ongoing interpretation through enforcement actions and case law. The Act creates temporal obligations: ongoing compliance, regular reporting, evolving codes of practice. For the field, it introduces a temporal marker: pre-Act AI training (unregulated) vs. post-Act AI training (regulated). This temporal divide will shape how AI art is historicized.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: The Act addresses a critical absence: the lack of legal framework for AI training data governance. It makes the previously invisible (AI model composition) partially visible (training data summaries). However, it does not fully address the absence of compensation mechanisms, enforcement capacity, or global coordination. The provisions make certain absences visible (we can now see that training data summaries are inadequate) while creating new ones (global enforcement gaps).

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Consensus-seeking through democratic process. EU legislation seeks political consensus across member states, parliament, and commission (trilogue process). The Act represents negotiated consensus between competing interests: AI industry (wanted minimal regulation), creative industries (wanted strong protections), civil society (wanted transparency and rights), and member states (varying positions). The result is a consensus document with deliberate ambiguities that will be resolved through implementation.
coherence.contestability: High. The provisions are contestable through: judicial review (CJEU), national court interpretation, legislative amendment, codes of practice negotiation, lobbying, and public advocacy. AI companies are already contesting the scope of training data summary requirements. Artist groups are contesting the adequacy of opt-out protections. The contestation is ongoing and productive.
coherence.forkability: Not forkable in the software sense — regulation is sovereign. However, the regulatory model is exportable: other jurisdictions can adopt similar provisions (and several are developing them). The Act sets a template that can be adapted, strengthened, or weakened by other regulatory systems. In this sense, the EU AI Act is a 'reference implementation' of AI training data regulation.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: The training data transparency principle — A(DAI) should make its knowledge sources visible and auditable, exceeding the Act's requirements as a values demonstration. The opt-out compliance infrastructure — A(DAI) must respect creator preferences about data inclusion from the start. The phased implementation approach — complex systems need graduated deployment. The multi-stakeholder governance concept — involving diverse voices in rule-making. The temporal marking concept (pre/post regulation) as a model for field periodization.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: The opt-out default — A(DAI) should adopt an opt-in model (explicit consent for inclusion) rather than opt-out (artists must actively refuse). The 'sufficiently detailed summary' vagueness — A(DAI) should provide full, granular transparency about its knowledge sources. The enforcement-gap tolerance — A(DAI) should build compliance into its architecture rather than relying on external enforcement. The exemption for open-source — A(DAI) should hold itself to the highest standard regardless of its licensing model.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: The EU AI Act establishes minimum standards; A(DAI) aspires to model maximum standards. The Act treats consent as opt-out; A(DAI) treats consent as opt-in. The Act regulates corporate AI from the outside; A(DAI) builds consent and transparency from the inside. The productive tension: A(DAI) can use the Act as a baseline while demonstrating what a genuinely consent-first, transparency-maximalist approach looks like. A(DAI) should be the system that makes the EU AI Act's provisions look conservative.

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: This IS the regulation. The EU AI Act is the regulatory framework against which other items in this research are measured. Key provisions: Article 53(1)(c) — copyright compliance policy; Article 53(1)(d) — training data summary; Article 50 — AI content labeling; Article 52 — transparency obligations. Penalties: up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global annual turnover. Enforcement begins August 2025 for GPAI provisions, August 2026 for full Act. The EU AI Office oversees compliance for general-purpose AI models.
regulatory_legal.ip_model: The Act reinforces the existing EU copyright framework (DSM Directive) and extends it to AI training contexts. It does not create new IP rights but clarifies that existing copyright applies to AI training data. The TDM exception (Article 4 DSM Directive) allows commercial data mining unless rights holders opt out — the AI Act requires AI providers to implement mechanisms to respect this opt-out. The Act maintains the European tradition of strong moral rights (attribution, integrity).
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Opt-out. Under the DSM Directive Article 4(3), rights holders must explicitly reserve their rights to prevent commercial text and data mining. The AI Act reinforces this opt-out framework: AI providers must respect rights reservations expressed in 'an appropriate manner, including machine-readable means.' This means artists must actively opt out (using robots.txt, ai.txt, or similar mechanisms) rather than being asked for permission. Artist advocacy groups argue this is inadequate — the burden should be on AI companies to obtain consent, not on artists to refuse.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: No platform dependency — this is sovereign regulation. However, enforcement effectiveness depends on cooperation from platforms and AI providers. The Act applies extraterritorially but enforcement against non-EU entities depends on their EU market presence (similar to GDPR enforcement challenges).
ecosystem.network_effects: Strong regulatory network effects. As EU compliance becomes standard, it raises the baseline globally (the 'Brussels Effect'). AI companies that comply for EU markets often apply the same standards globally (easier than maintaining two versions). Other jurisdictions adopting similar provisions amplify the effect. The regulatory framework creates a gravity well: the more entities comply, the more costly it is to not comply.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: The Act was developed during and after the NFT crash but is not directly related to crypto markets. It responds to the generative AI boom (2022-present). The post-crash relevance: the NFT crash demonstrated the consequences of unregulated digital asset markets. The AI Act represents a proactive regulatory approach to avoid a similar unregulated boom-and-bust cycle in generative AI. For digital art specifically, the Act arrives at a moment when the field is rebuilding post-crash with greater emphasis on sustainability and rights.
